Standard machine learning textbooks assume your rows are independent and
exchangeable. Müller and Guido say so explicitly: shuffle the dataset and you
lose nothing. Whether one tumour is benign doesn't depend on the previous
patient in the table.

Time series are the exact opposite. The load at 14:15 is nearly identical to
the load at 14:00, and knowing that is half the job. **The ordering is the
signal.** Which means every time a textbook shuffles the rows, you have to do
something else instead.

## What goes wrong, concretely

`train_test_split(X, y, random_state=42)` picks a random 75% of your rows for
training. On an hourly demand series, the training set now contains 14:00 and
16:00 while the test set contains 15:00.

Predicting 15:00 from its two immediate neighbours is not forecasting. It's
interpolation, and it's trivially easy. The model gets an R² of 0.99 and you
get a number that describes a task nobody will ever ask you to perform.

The failure is silent. Nothing crashes. The metric doesn't look suspicious —
it looks *great*, which is precisely why it survives review.

## The rule

Test data lies strictly in the future of training data. Always, per series.

```python
from_end = df.groupby(id_col).cumcount(ascending=False)
is_test = from_end < h
train, test = df[~is_test], df[is_test]
```

Counting backwards from the end of each group takes the tail of *h* points per
series regardless of how long each series is — which matters the moment you
have more than one, and they don't all start on the same date.

## The part that's still uncomfortable

A single holdout tells you how the model performed in one particular fortnight.
If that fortnight contained a mild winter, you've measured the weather, not the
model.

The honest version is rolling-origin backtesting: repeat the evaluation across
many cutoffs and look at the distribution of errors, not one number. It costs
more compute and it usually makes your results look worse.

That's the point.
